One table `theme_schedules(id, instance_id, label, theme_vector, starts_at, ends_at, created_at, revoked_at)`; the window rule lives in the DOMAIN (`parse_window` + `covers`), so the store and the router refuse a bad window with one sentence. Half-open by design (`starts_at <= at < ends_at`): the 25th then the 26th must not both apply for an instant, and an event must stop without an operator awake at midnight. RFC 3339 WITH OFFSET required — a bare local time is refused, because guessing the zone is how an event starts three hours early. Overlaps resolve to the window that STARTED LAST: a Christmas event inside a generic winter window is the more specific intent, whereas 'last written wins' would make the answer depend on the order an operator typed. Revoking sets `revoked_at` and keeps the row (a cancelled event is a fact worth reading back; same reason a saved query keeps its runs). Routes are admin-pseud only: GET/POST /federation/theme/schedule and DELETE /federation/theme/schedule/{id}; get_instance_theme serves the active window's vector plus a `schedule` object so a reader can tell a seasonal vector from the instance's own. Rejected: a config key (needs a restart to begin AND to end), overwriting instance_theme (loses the instance's own vector), a jobs row that mutates the theme (no window; the state it writes is indistinguishable from the operator's).

requirement: Compute and store a perceptual hash when media bytes are fetched, so the dedup search has something to match on
evidence: domain::media_resilience::difference_hash (dHash, 9x8 resample); app::media_fetch::{plan_fetch, classify_with_length, MediaFingerprint, content_hash}; db::media_resilience::record_fingerprint; 6 domain tests, 17 in crates/app/tests/media_fetch.rs, 5 persistence tests in crates/app/tests/media_resilience.rs
notes: Spec §32.7.2. Closes the gap M32-07a left: perceptual_hash was only ever written by a test, so the dedup search read an empty column. Three parts, each tested. (1) difference_hash computes a real 64-bit dHash - resample to a fixed 9x8 grid and compare each sampled pixel with the one to its left. The grid is fixed rather than derived from the input, which is the only reason hashes of two differently-sized copies of one image are comparable. My first implementation walked pixels until it had 64 bits, so a 16x16 image contributed only its first five rows and two images differing entirely below the top half hashed identically; only a test that varies the bottom of the image caught that. (2) plan_fetch is the SSRF guard on the fetch path, delegating to the existing scrapers::safety::is_forbidden_ip and is_local_hostname rather than carrying a second weaker list. It reads url.host() and matches url::Host::{Ipv4,Ipv6,Domain} - host_str().parse::<IpAddr>() returns None for every IPv6 literal because the string keeps its brackets, so the string form silently skipped [::1], [fe80::1] and [::ffff:127.0.0.1], exactly the addresses the check exists to catch; v4-mapped v6 is unwrapped with to_ipv4_mapped() on top. (3) record_fingerprint persists both hashes, refuses a missing row rather than reporting a fetch successful for a deleted reference, and stores perceptual_hash as NULL - never an empty string - when a body could not be decoded, because two empty strings are distance 0 apart and would merge every undecodable image into one reference. Two judgement calls worth recording: plain HTTP is allowed but reported as insecure rather than refused, because a mirror may simply serve images over HTTP and refusing would be a surprise; and perceptual_hash_algorithm now defaults to dhash, not phash, since dHash is the only algorithm this build computes and a default naming an unbuilt one makes a stock instance advertise a dedup it cannot perform. Spec §32.7.2's example and docs/config-reference.md were updated to match, and the enum's doc now says which variants are implemented. Image decoding was the open piece and landed in M32-07c: `image = "=0.25.6"` (pinned exactly because 0.25.7+ needs Rust 1.85 and the workspace declares rust-version 1.82), features png/jpeg/gif/webp/bmp, 14 transitive deps and no rayon. Still open: phash/whash/ahash remain unimplemented and are refused at compute time, audio_fingerprint is still unapplied to audio, and there is still no media job kind or fetch loop that drives the fetch path - the guard, the decode and the write are tested at their boundaries rather than by a queued job.

notes: Spec §32.7.2. Closes the last gap M32-07b named: a fetched JPEG/PNG could be content-hashed exactly but not perceptually, because nothing could turn bytes into pixels. fingerprint_encoded decodes to luma and fingers both hashes in one call; anything it cannot decode returns None so the caller stores the exact hash with a NULL perceptual one rather than a guess. Two decisions worth recording. And the bomb fixture originally emitted width*height zero bytes, making its own test 33 seconds; it now emits one real row, which is what a bomb looks like, and runs in 0.00s. requirement: Drive the fetch end to end in the worker so a media reference's hashes are computed from a real request
evidence: domain::jobs::JobKind::MediaFetch; app::media_job::{enqueue_media_fetch, handle_media_fetch}; app::worker dispatch arm; POST /api/v1/works/{id}/media-references enqueues; 12 end-to-end tests in crates/app/tests/media_fetch_job.rs (real HTTP server, real PNGs)
notes: Spec §32.7.2. Closes the last structural gap in the chain. M32-07b and M32-07c built the guard, the decoder and the write, and M32-07b's handoff recorded that record_fingerprint had NO production caller -- the 'a parser is not a feature' shape. This adds JobKind::MediaFetch (the job_kinds! macro emits the enum, ALL_KINDS, as_str and parse from one source, and kind_index/resource_class are exhaustive matches, so a new kind cannot be handled everywhere except the list), the worker handler, and the enqueue call in add_media_reference -- whose existing comment promised 'content hash computed async by the pipeline'. The handler runs the whole sequence: confirm the reference exists, take the first availability link by priority, refuse the URL, resolve the host, fetch with the instance client, classify before reading the body, read bounded, fingerprint, record. A job rather than request work because the URL is author-supplied and a slow or dead mirror must not hold an author's connection open; the payload names only the reference id, so no job row carries a URL and a corrected link is picked up by a retry. Classification is honoured, not lumped: 404/410 and a non-image are Fatal, 429/5xx and a connect or read failure are Transient, and a reference with no availability link is Fatal rather than a job that retries for the life of the instance. The body is read chunk-by-chunk against MAX_MEDIA_BYTES so a server that declares no Content-Length cannot send unbounded data. The most important decision: testing this against a loopback server required touching the SSRF guard, and my first cut took a trusted_address: Option<IpAddr> and branched AROUND the guard. It failed immediately -- the literal-address rejection lives inside plan_fetch, so the branch was never reached -- and it was wrong regardless, because a bypassed guard leaves a second, untested path through the most security-sensitive function in the chain. The working shape is plan_fetch_allowing(url, allow, timeout) with plan_fetch delegating to it with an empty slice: scheme, local-name and resolution checks all still run, production has exactly one path, and the allowlist applies to both the literal-address and the DNS-resolution check so the two cannot disagree. A test also had to stop deciding transience from error text: it looked for the substring 'transient' and failed on a correct message that said 'retrying'. The assertion is now on the error TYPE, with the prose kept in the assertion message. HandlerError gained Display and Error impls so it can be formatted normally. The 201 response now carries fingerprint_job_id. Gate: clippy 0/0, fmt clean, 82 suites with 0 failures.

requirement: Roadmap consensus repository: 12 previously untested functions with 48 tests across upsert_card/find_card_by_title_normalized/list_cards/arena_candidates/create_ballot/fetch_ballot/mark_voted/apply_elo_and_counters/record_move/list_moves/insert_suggestion/update_card_stage. The module was non-functional on PostgreSQL, the production backend: four separate decode failures, each in a function the public roadmap board calls on every page view. (1) row_to_card_postgres read matches_played/times_best/times_worst as i32 while every PG branch of list_cards selects them as CAST(... AS BIGINT), so every card failed to decode. (2) list_cards read created_at/updated_at (TIMESTAMPTZ) as String in all four branches. (3) fetch_ballot read the JSONB columns card_ids and served_elo as String. (4) list_moves read moved_by (UUID) and created_at (TIMESTAMPTZ) as String. All four fixed by rendering the non-text types as text in the PG SELECTs and reading the counters as i64; the SQLite arm is unchanged. Two design gaps are documented rather than fixed: the ON CONFLICT ... WHERE guard freezes a shipped or rejected card's entire row rather than only its stage, and normalize_title deletes punctuation instead of replacing it with a space so "Dark-Mode" is a duplicate of "DarkMode" but not of "Dark Mode".

requirement: Flexible bounties repository: 4 previously untested functions with 31 tests across create_bounty_typed/contribute_to_bounty/fetch_bounty/list_flexible_bounties, behind the economy page bounty board. The contribution ledger was broken on both backends. record_contribution inserted into bounty_contributions without its id column, and the two backends disagree about what that means: PostgreSQL rejects it outright (id TEXT PRIMARY KEY is NOT NULL), so a crowdfunded bounty accumulated funded_amount with no audit row at all on the production backend; SQLite accepts it and stores id = NULL, so the ledger had rows whose primary key was NULL and therefore could not identify a contribution. The caller discarded the error with `let _ =`, so neither backend reported anything. Both arms now supply a minted id and the swallowed error is logged. Verified by reverting the fix: the ledger tests fail on both backends, and the SQLite case needed a COUNT(id) assertion because a row-exists check passes there.

requirement: Instance taste settings: 4 previously untested functions (read/write/history/rollback) with 28 tests, behind the operator taste panel on /discovery. No production defect: the module already got the hard parts right -- every PostgreSQL SELECT renders UUID and TIMESTAMPTZ as text and widens INTEGER with ::bigint, the history insert and the settings upsert run in one transaction in that order because the settings row is a singleton and the history row is the only copy of the old values, the rows are sqlx::FromRow structs so a renamed column is a compile error, and the history is ordered by replaced_version rather than changed_at because now_rfc3339() has second precision. The tests pin those properties so none of them can be quietly undone, plus the version chain, the singleton invariant, the rollback-as-write semantics, and rolling back past version 1 landing on the config values rather than a hole. Its four pre-existing unit tests only covered the private row mappers, so nothing had ever reached the database.

notes: Spec 11.5 1.3. The counter is what lets an operator answer what the posture cost. A posture that reads what it was refused is a stronger claim than a boolean that ignored it, so it owes better accounting than the boolean did. The two numbers answer OPPOSITE questions and are deliberately not folded together: robots_overrides is 'is this instance ignoring sites?' and is something an operator may have to explain to a site's owner; robots_read_and_discarded is 'is MetadataOnly throwing away the dataset?' and non-zero means the posture is working as configured. requirement: A content fetch refused by posture is refused by name, is not retried, and a per-source override may only narrow and does not outlive its import run
evidence: robots::resolve_source_override -> Err(WideningRefused); narrows_or_equals over all nine pairs in BOTH crates; robots::caution_rank + robots::narrowest as the single order; config::RunScope (expires by being dropped, no clock); imports::run_scope_for selects the run's own non-persistent grants; imports::run_policy is the only way a run builds a policy; posture_for_source_in takes narrowest(run, file); catalogue reports robots_posture + instance_robots_posture + override_of; 15 mutations (E1-E9, F1-F6) in docs/plans/crawling-retention-preservation.md, all turn the suite red
notes: COMPLETE for the local build. Run scoping is a DROP, not a timer: run() builds a RunScope, hands it to run_policy, and the value dies with the run, so 'expired' and 'the run ended' are the same event and cannot drift. A run grant is OUTRANKED, not refused - posture_for_source_in takes narrowest(run, file), so a caller granting itself permissive against a strict config still fetches strict. TWO TRAPS, both hit here. (1) The rank order: low is the MOST cautious (Strict=0) and the rule is rank(asked) <= rank(instance). Strict=0 with >= reads correctly and is exactly backwards - it lets a strict instance accept a permissive override. Asserting one pair cannot catch an inverted order, so all nine are asserted twice. (2) A second rank was written in config.rs for the narrowest-of-two rule and it ranked Permissive as 0 - the same inversion in a second place. The fix was ONE exported caution_rank in the module that owns the enum. Also: a non-serde-defaulted map on a deny_unknown_fields struct made every existing config fail to parse ('missing field robots_posture_overrides'), which a purely additive option must never do. F4 and F5 SURVIVED and the finding was NOT a missing test: run_scope_for was REDUNDANT. posture_for_source already returns a persistent:false override on every lookup, so the run's grant and the file's answer were the same posture for the same source and the scope could not change any outcome. A path that cannot change a result is dead weight, so it was deleted - run_scope_for now returns an empty RunScope, the file answers, and F4/F5 are recorded as vacuous rather than quietly dropped. RunScope survives as the channel for mid-run grants from a caller, narrowed by narrowest(run, file) so it can never widen.

Three decisions worth naming. (a) The expression is re-joined from the positionals, so `dh q tag:naruto AND words:'>1000'` works without quoting the whole thing — but it is still percent-encoded whole, because `tag:a AND tag:b` contains the two characters (`&`, space) an encoder gets wrong. (b) `--cols`/`--fields` are restricted to the five columns a search *hit* carries (`rank`, `score`, `words`, `title`, `author`); `likes`/`status`/`updated`/`source` exist on a catalogue row and not on a hit, so offering them would print four blanks that read as 'this work has no likes' — the lie `--cols score` already refuses on the metric page. (c) The author needed one reader, not two: a hit calls the field `author_handle` where the catalogue calls it `author_text`, so the shared `rows()` reader takes either, which is also what makes `--jsonl` print `"author":"devwriter"` live. HALF TWO — the grammar the row names: `updated>=-7d` did not work. MEASURED on the live instance first: `/api/v1/search?q=updated%3A%3E%3D-7d` -> 422 'updated >= takes a YYYY-MM-DD date, got "-7d"'. The fix reuses the window grammar instead of parsing durations again: `window::instant` is now public, `window::boundary` calls it, and `parse_date_bound` calls it too, so `updated:>=-7d` and `--updated -7d..` land on the same day by construction. A test asserts exactly that agreement with a fixed clock, because two implementations that happen to agree today is the bug this avoids. The comparison is by day (`SUBSTR(column,1,10)`), so the resolved instant is truncated to its UTC date — a timestamp bound would make the same query mean different things at 00:01 and 23:59. The grammar is NOT relaxed (that rule is documented and deliberate): instead a term that names a known field and an operator is refused with the colon form, keyed on the vocabulary so `banana>3` and `tagged` stay text, and `tag>=romance` gets the sharper 'no ordering' message rather than advice that would earn a second error. requirement: peering is suggested by cosine similarity over that fingerprint, and a colliding hardcoded filter blocks it outright
evidence: crates/domain/src/peering.rs (assess/suggest/collisions/rank); crates/domain/src/taste_fingerprint.rs (declared `enforced` layer + build_with_rules); crates/db/src/peer_fingerprints.rs; crates/app/src/routes/peering.rs (GET /operator/peering/suggestions, PUT /operator/peering/fingerprints); crates/app/src/routes/well_known.rs publishes the layer; migrations/{sqlite,postgres}/0191_peer_fingerprints.sql; [discovery] peering_suggestions + enforced_rules
notes: Suki spec §16.2, over M69-01's published fingerprint. Cosine over the tag vector, the existing 0.25 floor, and the veto: a rule one side declares and the other does not is a BLOCK, and the check runs before any score is computed, because a number an operator can see is a number they can act on. The collision is symmetric (a peer that enforces MORE is also a collision: they refuse something this instance serves) and it names the rule and which side enforces it — 'blocked' without the rule is not actionable. Two instances that both enforce nothing do not collide: absence on both sides is agreement. The layer is DECLARED in config (`[discovery] enforced_rules`) and travels in the published document (`enforced`, serde-defaulted and omitted when empty). Deliberately not inferred, same rule as fandom adjacency (M64-08): a veto inferred from a sample can be outvoted by a larger sample. A peer whose document predates the field collides with nothing -- the honest reading of an unanswered question is that it was not answered, and the alternative (treating silence as 'enforces nothing') would veto every old peer on a guess. `rank()` drops collisions entirely rather than ranking them low: a suggestion list is a list an operator may pair with. `suggest()` keeps them and orders suggestions first, then vetoes, then near misses -- the veto outranks a near miss because a near miss is a maybe and a collision is an answer. The score rounds to four places and `+ 0.0` folds `-0.0`, which an orthogonal pair produced (a report printing '-0.000' reads as an arithmetic bug). Storage keeps the peer's document whole, keyed by the instance_id the document itself declares (a document filed under a host someone typed is a mis-filing), replaced on re-record (a fingerprint is a statement about now). OFF BY DEFAULT (`[discovery] peering_suggestions`); when off both doors answer 404, not 403. HONEST LIMITS: (1) nothing FETCHES a peer's document -- an operator records it, and a scheduler that walks known peers is not written; (2) the suggestion list is read-only: it does not write `federation_peers_v2` or set `auto_federate`, so a suggestion still has to be acted on by hand; (3) nothing throttles repeated comparisons, though the whole thing is a pure function over a handful of stored documents; (4) the veto compares rule NAMES only -- two instances that spell the same rule differently ('csam' vs 'child-safety') collide spuriously, and the honest fix is a controlled vocabulary for rule names rather than a fuzzy match, which would let a near-miss rule slip through a veto.

requirement: a signed taste passport moves a reader's taste and contribution history between instances, suki and darkhold alike
evidence: crates/domain/src/passport.rs (canonical_json, sign/sign_with_hex/verify, public_key_hex, normalised); crates/db/src/passports.rs; crates/app/src/routes/passport.rs (GET/POST/DELETE /me/passport, GET /me/passports); migrations/{sqlite,postgres}/0192_taste_passports.sql; [discovery] taste_passports + passport_key
notes: Suki spec §16.3. ed25519 over canonical JSON (sorted keys, no whitespace, integers only in the signed surface — floats are the part of JCS that is easiest to get subtly wrong, so the tag vector is basis points, not 0..1 reals). The signed bytes are produced by one function and both doors use it, which is why the round-trip test (export -> import) is the assertion that matters: a test that only checked 'export returns 200' would pass on two builds that disagree about the canonical form. The passport is a CLAIM: signed by the INSTANCE, not the reader, so it proves 'this instance said this about this handle' and nothing more. Its taste lands as `origin = 'imported'` taste_signals (§49.7's distinction), so local recomputation outvotes it as evidence accumulates — the passport bootstraps, it never replaces. `version` is checked and an unknown one is refused rather than partially read. Expiry is 180 days, checked in both directions (a document dated in the future is refused too, or an origin could set itself an arbitrary age). Caps: 200 tags, 100 sources, weights <= 10000 bp. Re-presenting a newer document from the same origin REPLACES the previous taste (two versions of one prior are not two priors) and replaces the receipt (one row per (account, origin)). Withdrawal deletes receipt AND signals, because evidence without provenance is not evidence. The export door carries the tag's CANONICAL NAME (via canonical_entities) rather than the local node id — an id means nothing to a receiver — and the PUBLIC key only: a door that echoed the seed would put a signing key in an HTTP response (there is a test). OFF BY DEFAULT (`[discovery] taste_passports`); export additionally needs `[discovery] passport_key` (hex 32 bytes, validated at LOAD so a typo is a startup failure rather than a reader's bug report), and without it the door answers 422 naming the setting. DEFECTS FOUND BY DOING THIS: (a) the first draft queried `chapter_revisions` and `taxonomy_nodes`, both renamed by 0122/0124 — every one of those queries would have failed on any live instance while a green local build said nothing; (b) the join table for a work's source does not exist (`library_items` carries both), so the first draft 500'd. HONEST LIMITS: (1) nothing fetches a peer's passport — a reader presents it, as the spec describes; (2) there is no UI for any of this (frontend rows own it); (3) the passport is not linked to a polaris-id identity, so 'this is the same person' rests on the reader choosing to present it — anything stronger would need the estate identity, which is out of this tree; (4) `favourite_sources` is exported but nothing consumes it yet (they are the sources the reader's own library copies came from, not everyone's).

requirement: a takedown is a tombstone that survives re-import, and the importer refuses the work citing the original
evidence: crates/domain/src/work_identity.rs (normalise, key, text_key); crates/db/src/tombstones.rs (Filing, file, refuse, list, withdraw); migrations/{sqlite,postgres}/0193_work_tombstones.sql; crates/app/src/imports.rs (tombstones_enabled); crates/app/src/routes/tombstones.rs; [discovery] work_tombstones
notes: Suki spec §5.5 and §13.2 step 3. WHAT MAKES TWO COPIES THE SAME WORK: title + author + language, normalised (NFKD, lowercase, marks dropped, punctuation and spacing collapsed), hashed to 32 hex. NOT the URL — a takedown that stops one string stops one import, and the whole failure is the work coming back from a mirror tomorrow. NOT the body: imports arrive without bodies, a body legitimately changes when the author edits a chapter, and two mirrors rarely carry byte-identical text. `text_key` exists for a later second key on the same tombstone; it is not what the importer checks. WHAT NORMALISATION DOES NOT DO: it does not remove words or reorder them, so 'The Storm, part 2' and 'The Storm' are different works — an over-matching tombstone removes a sequel nobody complained about, which is worse than a second filing. An empty author is NOT a wildcard: treating a missing author as 'any author' would tombstone every work with that title. The separator is the unit separator, which `normalise` strips, so ('a b','c') cannot collide with ('a','b c'). DEFECT FOUND BY DOING THIS: the first draft dropped combining marks WITHOUT decomposing, so 'Á' as one code point and 'A'+acute were two different keys — the accent test caught it, and the fix is NFKD before lowercasing. That failure mode matters because the importer emits whichever spelling the source served. notes: Concord card '[I] Seed sets'. `seed=a1,a2,a3` ranks by the UNION of the seeds' vocabulary and excludes every seed from the results. Union, not intersection: the works that describe one subgenre do not share a vocabulary — one carries `gamer`, another `litrpg` — so requiring all would find nothing. Duplicates collapse, so a word two seeds share is ONE vote: the seed is the set's vocabulary, not a weighted sum of five titles, and weighting by repetition would let the longest summary dominate. The author bonus survives only when every seed shares one author — five works by five authors are not evidence of an author a reader likes. The set spends ONE budget: preselection tokens are six per seed up to twelve total in the order the reader named them, because twenty short seeds would otherwise preselect on a hundred words, which is the catalogue rather than a taste. Cap is 20 seeds, refused with a sentence ('beyond that the union stops describing a taste and starts describing the catalogue'): a query-cost bound, not a taste limit. Ambiguity is refused PER NAME — 'seed "X": N rows match, pick one by id' plus six candidates — because a set query with one ambiguous name would otherwise print candidates with no clue which name produced them. The response's `seed` object carries the joined ids and 'Title (+N more)' so a client can say what it ranked by. Concord card '[M] Operator taste'. `POST|GET|DELETE /federation/theme/operator` (admin, pseud door like the rest of that router): the operator names a shelf, every line is resolved the same way `?seed=` resolves one (catalogue row, then stored external evidence by id), and the instance theme is derived from the resolved seeds' TAGS as its own published object. PUBLISHED, NOT BLENDED, is the row's whole point: `GET /federation/theme` now returns `source` (season|operator|bookmarks|none), the effective vector, the shelf's own `top_tags`/`seed_count`/`resolved_count`, AND `computed_vector` beside it — so a reader can tell 'the operator wants this' from 'our readers happen to like this'. Blending would have made the claim unfalsifiable. PRECEDENCE, decided once in `domain::operator_theme::precedence`: season > operator shelf > bookmarks > none. A season is an event and expires; the shelf is what the instance is FOR; bookmarks are what its readers happen to like — putting bookmarks above the shelf would let the audience contradict the operator by accident. WEIGHTING: each tag counts once per CONTRIBUTING seed (dedupe inside a seed, so a work tagged `dark` twice is one work saying it once), weight = count / contributing seeds — adding a sixth seed must not dilute the first five, because the vector describes the shelf, not a share of a pie that grows. A seed with no tags contributes nothing and does not become the denominator. Every line is kept with its outcome: '3 posted / 2 used' plus the reason for the third is the useful fact, and a response that listed only the two would be indistinguishable from a shelf of two. A shelf where NO line carries a tag is REFUSED with a sentence naming the count ('theme: none of the 2 seeds carries a tag — a shelf with no tags states nothing this instance can act on') rather than stored as an empty claim. Storage is one row per instance, REPLACED on re-post (two statements of what an instance is for cannot both be true) and deletable so it can go back to bookmarks; DELETE reports the source it falls back to, including an already-open season — answering `none` while an event runs would be a small lie in the one response whose job is to say where the theme comes from.

requirement: A general plugin system — third-party code loaded into the server, distributed through a marketplace of installable packages — is evaluated and rejected; the extension surface is declarative documents plus documented integration points.
notes: Rejected in ADR 0005, and recorded here so the question does not get re-opened as if it had never been answered. The reasons are specific to this product rather than aesthetic: (1) the reader is server-rendered HTML that works without JavaScript (DM5-01), so a plugin model that means the browser executes author code contradicts a stated floor; (2) erasure is an invariant with a gate that names every account-bearing column (M45-64) — a third party holding reader data breaks erasure in a way no test in this suite can see; (3) route inventory is a complete statement about what the server does, and plugin routes end it; (4) a plugin API is a permanent compatibility promise, while the module registry gives the same freedom internally with none of it; (5) a marketplace is a supply chain, and WordPress is the worked example of a successful one becoming a security disaster. The alternatives considered and rejected are in the ADR, including WASM sandboxing, which solves untrusted execution but not untrusted DATA.

requirement: §21.4's execution sandbox: `wasmi` with fuel, memory ceilings, output limits, host-call limits, bounded concurrency, hard wall-clock termination, host-I/O timeouts, and revocation that stops a running package.
evidence: cargo test -p darkhold-sandbox (13 passed) · cargo test -p darkhold-app --test m16_06_sandbox_route (5 passed) · route_inventory 5/5 · clippy -D warnings · gate.sh repo ok
notes: New crate `crates/sandbox` (`darkhold-sandbox`), `wasmi` 2.x, with one caller: `POST /api/v1/operator/sandbox/run` (operator-only, inside the /api/v1 nest so it carries the session middleware and CSRF). Each ceiling is enforced AND has a module that hits it: fuel (a tight loop with no imports — the only ceiling that can stop one), memory (StoreLimits with `trap_on_grow_failure`, so a denied grow reports `memory` instead of the module's own `out of bounds memory access`), host calls (counted, refused past the budget), output (a refused write appends nothing — a half-written document is worse than none), wall clock (checked before the call, inside every host import and after it), host-I/O timeout (measured per call, after the work, because checking before would measure the wrong interval), concurrency (Concurrency holds an AtomicUsize bound per AppState, refusing with 429 + retry hint rather than queueing), and revocation (an AtomicBool polled at every host call and once before entry). HONEST LIMITS, named rather than papered over: `wasmi` has no epoch interrupt, so a module that never calls the host cannot be stopped by the clock — it is stopped by fuel, which is why fuel is a ceiling and not an estimate; and `checkpoint` is the import that makes a long run interruptible, so an extension that never calls it is bounded only by fuel. The host imports are `write` and `checkpoint`; real host I/O does not exist yet, so `host_call_timeout` measures the boundary the real imports will use. No subscription uplift is applied at the door: the caller passes the manifest's own ceilings, so the sandbox enforces policy it was given and invents none. Mutations: gate removed → reader got 200; `trap_on_grow_failure` dropped → memory reported as a plain trap; per-call budget ignored → HostTimeout never fired; concurrency refusal removed → a full sandbox ran the module anyway. Unblocks M16-07 (automated checks for a submission), M16-08 and M16-12.

Install counts are COUNT(*) WHERE uninstalled_at IS NULL at read time -- a census, so reinstalling cannot inflate it and the number can go down. Update policy (pinned|minor|any) resolves with domain code, moves forward only, and refuses a move that widens the grant, naming only the new capabilities. Ratings are one per scope per package, 1-5 with no zero ('no opinion' is the absence of a row), require an active install, and record the version rated; aggregates publish 'no ratings yet' rather than 0.0. requirement: §21.9's paid marketplace, separate from credits: purchases, entitlements, refunds, developer revenue accounting, optional processor-backed payouts, the 85/15 reference split, and operator tax/invoicing setup.
evidence: cargo test -p darkhold-domain --lib payments (9 passed) · cargo test -p darkhold-app --test m16_11_payments (5 passed) · cargo test -p darkhold-db --test payments_two_engines (3 passed on SQLite and 3 on PostgreSQL 55433) · route_inventory 5 · migration_catalogue 6 · snapshot 2689/369 · clippy -D warnings · gate ledger/repo
notes: Separate from credits by construction: payments/refunds/extension_prices/operator_tax_profile reference no credit balance, and credits (M45-18) reference nothing here. Purchase records a payment in state 'pending' and grants nothing; capture is the moment money exists and the only moment access is granted (grant_extension) and the seller's share is posted (85/15 via Rules::split on the NET of tax, remainder to the developer so the halves sum to the gross). Refunds are cumulative in one column with the SQL guard `refunded_minor + amount <= amount_minor`, so an over-refund is impossible even if a caller skips the domain check; a FULL refund revokes the grant and reverses the seller's share, a PARTIAL one does neither (documented: a goodwill refund is not a return). Tax is computed inclusive from a stored profile (rate_bp, half-up) so net + tax == gross and invoices reconcile; setting a profile is not registering or filing tax and the response says so. The processor port is Processor::Manual: the only honest processor when no provider exists -- a receipt with captured:false and a pending payment an operator settles against a bank transfer, and a provider-backed processor only has to return captured:true. Money columns are BIGINT (INT4 overflows at ~21M euros): the two-engine test caught three INT4 decode failures before that change, which is the same class of bug the gallery row hit. Known gaps: no invoice document rendering (the identity and rate are stored, no PDF), no payout accounting for extensions (author_earnings_ledger is credited and the existing request_payout path settles it), no processor webhook.

requirement: §21's acceptance list: infinite loops terminate, memory excess fails safely, host APIs enforce permission denial, revoked packages stop running, uninstall removes grants, reset remains reachable after a broken theme, forks keep attribution and request their own grants, and custom engines and recipes honour opt-out.
evidence: cargo test -p darkhold-app --test m16_12_acceptance (9 passed, one per claim) · cargo test -p darkhold-domain --lib recipe_document (9 passed) · cargo test -p darkhold-sandbox (revocation_stops_a_running_module_at_its_next_host_call) · route_inventory 5 · migration_catalogue 6 · snapshot 2711/372 · clippy -D warnings · gate ledger/repo
notes: Every claim in the list now has a test that names it. The last clause is the one that needed a decision rather than a test: 'custom engines and recipes honour opt-out' is TWO different answers. An engine runs code or drives a process outside the host, so `custom_processing: refuse` governs it and `POST /extensions/{slug}/apply-recipe` refuses with the setting's own name. A declarative recipe composes strategies the instance already runs, so it hands nothing outside and consent does NOT govern it -- refusing an opted-out reader there would be a false positive that teaches readers the setting is noise. That is not a convention: `crates/domain/src/recipe_document.rs` gives a recipe a closed schema (`stages[{strategy, weight}]`, weights in (0,1], at most 8, no duplicate strategy), so a document that could carry an endpoint is refused BY NAME, which is what makes 'a recipe processes nothing' structural. `processing(category)` is the one place that answers which categories run, and the route asks it before reading anything out of the body. Applying a recipe stores it as the reader's own row via the existing recipe store, so 'apply' has a visible outcome. Recipe strategy names are validated against `rec_engine::available_strategies()` rather than a second list in the domain, because two lists drift the moment a strategy is added. Gaps: the instance's blend does not yet read recipe documents (M69/M64 own that), so an applied recipe is stored and validated but does not change the feed; engine packages are refused the deny-listed path but there is no engine runner to hand a package to.
gates: 9 acceptance + 9 recipe-domain + sandbox revocation

requirement: §21.7's theme model beyond one stylesheet: design tokens, constrained layout slots, scoped styling, preview, reset, safe mode, accessibility checks — and the rule that a theme cannot hide the positivity filter status, the feedback mechanism, the safety controls or the extension management interface.
evidence: cargo test -p darkhold-domain --lib theme_model (12 passed) · cargo test -p darkhold-app --test m16_13_themes (6 passed) · cargo test -p darkhold-db --test themes_two_engines (3 passed on SQLite and 3 on PostgreSQL 55433) · route_inventory 5 · migration_catalogue 6 · snapshot 2711/372 · clippy -D warnings · gate ledger/repo
notes: A theme is data, not a document: a closed ten-token palette (colours as #rrggbb, measure in ch bounded 30..120) and, for an instance theme only, a placement per slot from a closed set (stacked|inline|aside|full). `declarations()` emits custom properties and nothing else, so a theme has no selector to aim -- it cannot target an element, therefore cannot hide one. Slots cannot be removed: a missing slot means core, and a renderer walks `Slot::all()`. Scope: an instance theme is the operator's (checked before anything is written) and may lay out; a reader theme is palette-only and keeps the instance's layout. Preview is a (theme, session) row with an expiry checked server-side, so a preview the client remembers is not enough. Reset DELETEs the published row rather than writing the defaults; a save demotes a published theme to draft, because the bytes approved are not the bytes just written. Safe mode is one row and beats everything including a live preview -- the preview is the theme most likely to be broken. Accessibility: WCAG 2.2 AA contrast computed in the crate from the tokens themselves; 4.5:1 for body pairs, and publish REFUSES a failing theme (save refuses too, so the form shows the failure live). `--dh-border` is deliberately not an enforced pair: a hairline divider is decoration rather than a WCAG 1.4.11 object, and enforcing it would make every theme garish or refused. Cannot-hide: the four protected surfaces (positivity status, feedback, safety controls, extension management) each publish a positional mechanism -- host document, outside a shadow-root theme boundary, `all: revert`, flow-only placements -- and `GET /themes/effective` returns that list so the renderer has the contract. HONEST GAP: the renderer half is not verified in this tree -- there is no frontend test asserting the four surfaces sit outside the theme root, and no theme console UI; the model makes hiding inexpressible, but 'the shell renders them outside' is a contract the SPA must satisfy and nobody has proven it does.
gates: 12 domain + 6 http + 3 two-engine on both engines

requirement: §21.8's operational half: rotating secrets, a per-subscription rate limit, and auto-disable of a subscription that keeps failing.
evidence: cargo test -p darkhold-domain --lib webhook (11 passed) · cargo test -p darkhold-app --test m16_14_webhooks (7 passed, incl. 2 that run the real delivery loop against a local receiver) · cargo test -p darkhold-db --test webhooks_two_engines (1 passed on SQLite and 1 on PostgreSQL 55433) · route_inventory 5 · migration_catalogue 6 · snapshot 2695/369 · clippy -D warnings · gate ledger/repo
notes: Rotation: `POST /me/webhooks/{id}/rotate` returns the new secret once and moves the old one to `previous_secret` with `rotated_at`; `admissible_keys` admits both for 24h, so a subscriber mid-deploy keeps verifying instead of failing twenty times and switching itself off. The delivery header carries `v1=<current>,v0=<previous>` during the window and the log records only the current signature. Rate limit: `rate_per_minute` (default 60) per subscription, counted from `webhook_deliveries` in the last minute EXCLUDING throttled rows -- counting them would let the limiter consume its own budget and extend its own silence. A throttled attempt is recorded, not dropped, because an absent delivery reads as an outage. Breaker: 20 consecutive failures in `record_failure` (the domain's `Breaker`, not the store) flips `active=0` and writes `disabled_at`/`disabled_reason`; a success resets the count, a success while disabled does not resurrect the endpoint (only `POST /operator/webhooks/{id}/enable` does, and it is owner/operator-gated). `list_all_active_webhooks` already filters `active = 1`, so a switched-off endpoint receives nothing and cannot fail again. Operator view `GET /operator/webhooks` deliberately omits secrets: an operator needs to know an endpoint is failing, not to forge its deliveries. Known gaps: no backoff schedule of its own (retries remain the outbox's subject, `attempt` is still 1); no per-event-type limit (the limit is per subscription, which is what the requirement asks); no notification to the owner when the breaker switches them off (the state is visible in `GET /me/webhooks` and in the operator view, but nobody is told).
gates: 11 domain + 7 http (2 wired) + 1 two-engine on both engines
